items.title: 52035_Eddie Durham oral history interview
items.q: and then ran into Don Redman, and Don Redman was doing six-part harmony

ctx.x: Yeah. So finally I got away from all that. And so that's what I learned there. It got so they couldn't offer me much and (unintelligible) what I got here, I got a foundation, so I went creating for myself. So when I came to New York, that's when I run into guys like Bingie Madison, who was voicing, and then ran into Don Redman, and Don Redman was doing six-part harmony, and that's when -- and when I heard his (unintelligible) I said, what do you name this chord? He says, it's just a double the minute. Nobody's…

So, now I got some things where you can do seven-part harmony and that sounds all right, but you need instrumentation to do it. So I made one for Battles with his six saxes, top to bottom, all six-part harmony, commercial melody. That was about three years ago, it's still in the books.
